# Performance History

How fast BlitzLLVM is, and what each performance change did to it. Every row is a revision of the compiler and runtime, oldest first: the baseline at the top, the original Blitz3D, then every merged change that affects performance. A row shows the numbers **after** its change, and in brackets the change against the row above it, so there is no separate "before" column. 📈 is better, 📉 is worse and ➖ is the same (a change of the mean under 3%, or one smaller than two standard deviations of the difference of the two rows). Last updated 2026-10-28.

## How the numbers are made

* Every benchmark is built with the compiler of the commit of that row (its default options) and run **10 times**. A number is the **mean** of the runs, followed by ± the standard deviation. All runs are in `benchmarks/history/` (JSON).
* The programs are the ones of the latest `root` (`benchmarks/`, run by `benchmarks/history.py`), so every compiler runs the same program. Where an old compiler can not build the BlitzLLVM include (no `Microseconds`, no `Stats3D`), the include for the original Blitz3D is used: its timer has a resolution of a millisecond and it has no draw counters. Programs are shown as `n/a` where a compiler can not build or run them.
* A change in brackets is against the last row above that has a number, so after a run of `n/a` rows it spans several revisions.
* Results are sectioned by **machine definition**: CPU, GPU, OS and version, RAM, VRAM and the renderer or converter. Numbers of different machine definitions can not be compared.
* The original Blitz3D 1.118 is a Windows program. Here it runs under Wine, and its Direct3D 7 is converted to OpenGL by wined3d on llvmpipe. That is only there to have a number to put next to the others (and for the pixel comparisons); it is **not** what the original does on a real computer.
* llvmpipe is a software rasterizer: most of a frame is the CPU drawing pixels, so changes that save GPU work or draw calls barely show. A real GPU is needed for those; those runs have to be added as a machine definition of their own.
* **TODO**: neighbouring rows are tested one pair at a time, so with this many rows a few false 📈/📉 are expected at p < 0.01; a correction for the number of comparisons (or one regression over all rows) would be better, and more runs make the test stronger.
* To rebuild this page after a merge that affects performance: build the compiler, run `python3 benchmarks/history.py --blitzcc PATH --label NAME`, add the revision to `benchmarks/history/revisions.json` and run `python3 benchmarks/history_page.py`.

## Machine 2: Native Vulkan on a real GPU

| | |
| --- | --- |
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D |
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080 SUPER |
| OS and version | Windows 11 Pro 24H2 (10.0.26100) |
| RAM | 64 GB DDR5-6400 (61.6 GB usable) |
| VRAM | 16 GB |
| Renderer / converter | Vulkan, NVIDIA driver (native) |

Only a few rows exist for this machine definition so far (runs on it are queued one at a time). More are to be added with `benchmarks/history.py`.

### Benchmarks

#### Many lights

| Date, commit | Results |
| --- | --- |
| 2026-10-27<br>[#209](https://github.com/Xaymar/BlitzLLVM/pull/209) merged<br>[`7294987d`](https://github.com/Xaymar/BlitzLLVM/commit/7294987d) | 8 lights: 0.288 ms (before 0.245 ms, within noise) ➖<br>32 lights: 0.382 ms (before 0.248 ms, +54%) 📉<br>127 lights: 0.825 ms (before 0.248 ms, +233%) 📉 |
| 2026-10-27<br>[#249](https://github.com/Xaymar/BlitzLLVM/pull/249) merged<br>[`d779c7c1`](https://github.com/Xaymar/BlitzLLVM/commit/d779c7c1) | 8 lights: 0.303 ms (before 0.288 ms, within noise) ➖<br>32 lights: 0.275 ms (-28%) 📈<br>127 lights: 0.293 ms (-64%) 📈<br>127 lights, one moving: 0.843 ms (+3%) ➖ |

`benchmarks/many_lights.bb`, 5000 cubes, 640x360 windowed, no vsync, CPU submit time per frame. With one moving light all picks are redone: still about 2.9x slower than before #209 (0.287 ms to 0.843 ms). Static lights are back near the baseline (0.248 ms to 0.293 ms, +18%). Two alternating passes each, timer noise about 0.03 ms. Taken from the descriptions of those pull requests.

## Experiments that did not help

Measured on a real GPU system and dropped (from the pull requests): the world matrix reuse of #157 (no gain), more swapchain images and mailbox present mode of #185 (mailbox 41% slower), splitting the entity into a hot and a cold part (about 2%), batching image uploads (-0.3%), full or thin LTO of the runtime (not smaller than section GC, 16-32 s compile time) and `--fast-math full` as the default (breaks NaN checks).
